title: Keep your footing
hook: turn outward to please someone and you've lost your footing (Enchiridion 23)

segments.voice: Yesterday: expect to be laughed at. Your line was hold to it. Did you keep a practice quietly, with no raised eyebrow? Day three hundred fifty-five.
screen: `EXPECT TO BE LAUGHED AT — HOLD TO IT.`

segments.voice: You're in a meeting and your manager floats an idea you think won't work. You open your mouth to say so. Then you see their face, hopeful, a little proud, and you hear yourself say: yeah, that could be great. Or you're at a party, and someone makes a joke about a group of people, and you laugh along, a beat late, because everyone else did. Afterward there's a small wobble, as if the floor had tilted. Section twenty-three of the handbook is two sentences long, and it names that wobble exactly. Today: keep your footing.
screen: `YEAH, THAT COULD BE GREAT.` → `LAUGHING A BEAT LATE.` → `THE FLOOR TILTS.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis. If it ever happens, Epictetus says, that you turn outward because you want to please someone, know that you've lost your footing. The Greek word is enstasis: a stance, a way of standing, a plan of life you've set yourself in. The moment you face outward to win approval, you've stepped off it. Second, what pleasing isn't. Kindness isn't the problem. Bringing a friend soup, choosing the restaurant your partner likes, laughing at a child's bad joke: those can all come from your own footing. The trouble is when the aim shifts from doing right to being liked, and you start bending your words to someone else's face. Third, the remedy. Be content, he says, in everything, simply to be a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. And if you also want to seem one, seem one to yourself. That's enough. It's a strangely freeing sentence. You need one witness, and you already have them. Fourth, the practice in real life. Keeping your footing doesn't mean saying every harsh thing you think. In the meeting, it might sound like: I'm not sure that will work, can I say why? At the party, it might be not laughing, and changing the subject. Quiet, small, honest. People-pleasing usually feels like it buys peace. Epictetus thinks the price is higher than it looks. Each time we tilt toward someone's approval, we hand them a little of the ground we stand on. Keep it.
screen: `TURNED OUTWARD TO PLEASE.` · `ENSTASIS: YOUR STANCE.` · `SEEM SO TO YOURSELF.` · `QUIET, SMALL, HONEST.` · then, large: `KEEP MY FOOTING.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can, or plant your feet flat on the floor where you sit. Feel your weight, even, on both feet. Now bring to mind a person you tend to bend toward: a boss, a parent, a friend whose approval you want. Picture them in front of you. Notice whether your body leans, even slightly. Come back to center. Feel both feet again. Picture saying one honest, kind sentence to them, from right here. The bell holds the time.
Keep your footing. Epictetus' warning: turn outward to please someone and you've stepped off your stance; be content to be what you are, in your own eyes. Today's word.
Your line: keep my footing. Skip one people-pleasing move today, the automatic yes, the late laugh, and say one honest, kind thing instead. Day three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when they are shaping their words to win someone's approval, and return to saying what they actually think, kindly.
